AI expansion prompts new approaches to data center financing strategies
AI-driven growth is changing how data centers secure funding for multi-phase developments requiring large investments. Industry leaders say flexible financing models are needed to meet evolving project demands.
The rapid growth of artificial intelligence infrastructure is prompting changes in how data centers are financed, according to an Oct. 7 article from BBVA. Large-scale developments now often require multi-billion-dollar investments and are constructed over several years, with sponsors funding campuses that expand in phases as demand increases.
This shift means financing models must evolve alongside the projects themselves. Sponsors typically begin with land and site infrastructure before moving into initial buildings, adding capacity as customer needs develop. Each stage introduces different capital requirements and construction milestones, making flexibility a key consideration.
“Five years ago, you were looking at a very different type of data center project,” Michael Lardieri, Managing Director, Institutional Client & Financial Sponsors at BBVA USA, said. “Today we're talking about campuses that can require billions of dollars of investment and are being developed in multiple phases. That changes how sponsors think about capital and what they need from their banks.”
Lardieri also said that clients now prioritize not just access to capital, but certainty around its availability within project timelines: “Clients don't only want to know whether the capital is available,” he said. “They want confidence that it can be delivered on the timeline the project requires. As the market has accelerated, that certainty has become increasingly important.”
Infrastructure elements such as power capacity play a significant role in both development timing and financing decisions for large AI-oriented facilities. The need for reliable electricity supply influences when projects can proceed and when funds must be deployed.
As AI continues to drive investment in digital infrastructure, financial institutions face challenges matching substantial amounts of capital with projects built at larger scales under tighter deadlines. This evolving landscape is making data center financing more dynamic for both sponsors and lenders.
